## Abstract

## Purpose

To characterize the clinical presentation, disease course, and outcomes of patients with concurrent primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and celiac disease (CeD), including those with concomitant inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

## Methods

Retrospective EHR analysis (MGB RPDR, BIDMC Celiac Center, All of Us) identified patients with confirmed PSC and CeD (ICD-10, encounter threshold > 1, validated clinically/serologically/histologically). Primary outcomes were hepatic complications and time to liver transplantation, compared against two 3:1 age-matched cohorts (PSC + IBD, n = 54; PSC-only, n = 54).

## Results

Among 7.5 million patients in RPDR, 18,375 had CeD and 992 had PSC, with 13 observed cases of overlap versus 2.43 expected (OR 5.35, 95% CI 3.08–9.30; p < 0.001). Eighteen patients met full inclusion criteria (67% male, 94% White, mean age 47.8 years at PSC diagnosis). IBD was present in 72%, predominantly Ulcerative Colitis (56%). With high gluten-free diet adherence (89%), hepatic complications occurred in 89% of patients, with cirrhosis in 50%. Liver transplantation was required in 22%, at a mean of 5.4 years from PSC diagnosis among transplants with dated intervals, with no posttransplant PSC recurrence observed among the 4 transplanted patients. Compared with matched PSC + IBD (n = 54) and PSC-only (n = 54) control cohorts, liver transplantation was numerically more frequent in the PSC + CeD cohort than in either control cohort, though this difference did not reach significance (22.2% vs 5.6% vs 13.0%; chi-square p = 0.127).

## Conclusion

PSC and CeD co-occur at a significantly higher frequency than expected, suggesting shared autoimmune pathogenic mechanisms. The substantial hepatic complication burden and frequent IBD co-occurrence highlight the clinical importance of this overlap and the need for multidisciplinary management and routine autoimmune screening in affected patients. Matched-cohort comparisons further suggest a numerically elevated, though not statistically significant, risk of liver transplantation in PSC + CeD patients relative to PSC + IBD patients without celiac disease, alongside a significantly elevated risk of cirrhosis and PSC–autoimmune hepatitis overlap.

## Introduction

<!-- Page 3 -->


The coexistence of multiple immune-mediated diseases within a single patient is increasingly recognized as a clinically significant phenomenon, yet the implications of such overlap often remain poorly understood both with regard to insights into clinical care and potentially disease pathophysiology. Among these, the intersection of celiac disease (CeD) and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) presents a compelling but underexplored area of study. In addition, as PSC most often accompanies ulcerative colitis [1], consequently for many individuals, this represents an overlapping occurrence of three autoimmune diseases. While each condition is individually associated with autoimmune dysregulation and gastrointestinal morbidity, their concurrent presence raises important questions about shared pathophysiological mechanisms and compounded clinical burden. Case reports and small series have hinted at a potential association, suggesting that undiagnosed celiac disease may exacerbate malabsorptive symptoms or alter the disease trajectory in PSC [2]. However, the absence of larger, outcome-driven studies leaves clinicians without clear guidance for managing this overlap.

Both PSC and CeD are chronic immune-mediated disorders with overlapping pathogenetic features. PSC is an autoimmune cholestatic liver disease often linked with Inflammatory Bowel Disease usually UC [1], and celiac disease is an HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) ‐associated enteropathy triggered by gluten [3]. Familial reports hint at a shared predisposition: for example, two sisters with ulcerative colitis, PSC, and silent celiac disease both carried HLA‐DR3/DQ2 risk haplotypes [4]. Early case series also noted a suspected immunologic connection documented three PSC patients who concurrently had celiac disease and malabsorption [9]. In those cases, initiating a gluten‐free diet reversed steatorrhea but did not alter the underlying cholangiopathy [9]. Such observations suggest that these diseases may share immune pathways (e.g. gut‐derived immune activation) even though their precise relationship remains unclear [5].

PSC itself is an uncommon but severe disorder; population-based studies report a pooled incidence in the range of 0 to 1.58 per 100,000 person-years, with a mean/median estimate of 0.7–0.8 per 100,000 person-years [6], and a natural history marked by progressive biliary fibrosis, recurrent cholangitis, and eventual cirrhosis or cholangiocarcinoma in a substantial minority of patients [1]. The great majority of PSC occurs alongside IBD, chiefly ulcerative colitis, and this IBD association is itself understood to influence colorectal cancer surveillance needs and long-term hepatic prognosis [1]. Celiac disease, by contrast, is far more prevalent in the general population (estimated at approximately 1% worldwide) but has traditionally been considered a distinct enteropathy with a separate genetic architecture, even though it shares the same HLA-DQ2/DQ8 predisposing haplotypes implicated in other PSC-associated autoimmune conditions [3, 4]. Population-level data quantifying how much more often CeD and PSC cooccur than chance would predict have only recently become available, and, to our knowledge, no prior study has benchmarked the hepatic outcomes of patients with this overlap against outcome data from patients with PSC alone or PSC with IBD but without celiac disease. This absence of a comparatorcontrolled outcomes analysis has left open the basic clinical question of whether celiac disease overlap meaningfully changes the trajectory of PSC-related liver disease, or whether the apparent severity of reported cases instead reflects small, uncontrolled case series and referral bias.

This retrospective multi-institutional study addresses this gap in two parts. First, we characterize the clinical presentation, disease course, and outcomes of patients with concurrent PSC and CeD, including those with concomitant UC, in a cohort identified across three data sources. Second, to determine whether this overlap is associated with a distinct clinical trajectory rather than simply reflecting the natural history of PSC, we benchmark these outcomes against two independently identified comparator cohorts drawn from the same registry and matched 3:1 to the primary cohort on sex and approximate age at PSC diagnosis: patients with PSC and IBD without celiac disease, and patients with PSC alone without IBD or celiac disease. Together, these analyses aim to address a gap in the literature and to clarify whether increased clinical vigilance, and a specific need for autoimmune cross-screening, is warranted in this rare disease combination.

## Methods

## Study Design and Participant Selection

We conducted a retrospective analysis using electronic health records from three sources: the Mass General Brigham Research Patient Data Registry (RPDR; >7.5 million patients), the Celiac Center at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), and the All of Us Research Program (~ 630,000 participants), a worldwide NIH-managed cohort. Each source provided structured EHR data including demographics, diagnostic codes, laboratory results, and treatment histories.

Eligible patients had confirmed diagnoses of both primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and celiac disease (CeD), defined by ICD-10 codes (encounter threshold > 1, to minimize rule-out diagnoses or coding errors) and validated by clinical, serologic, or histologic evidence in the medical record; RPDRidentified cases additionally underwent manual chart review to confirm diagnostic accuracy. Patients were excluded for secondary sclerosing cholangitis or incomplete diagnostic confirmation of either condition.

## Data Collection and Variables

Extracted data included age at diagnosis, sex, and ethnicity. Age at diagnosis was recorded for both PSC and CeD, and the interval between diagnoses (age at PSC diagnosis minus age at CeD diagnosis) was calculated to characterize temporal sequence. Gluten-free diet adherence was obtained from clinical documentation, given its relevance as a modifiable management factor.

To assess whether PSC-CeD co-occurrence exceeded chance expectations, we calculated the expected number of overlapping cases assuming independence: (N�ₑ𝒹 × Nₚₛ𝒸)/Nₜₒₜₐₗ, where Nₚₛ𝒸 and N�ₑ𝒹 are the numbers of patients with PSC and CeD, respectively, and Nₜₒₜₐₗ is the total registry population. Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated to quantify and test the significance of this association.

Primary outcome measures included major hepatic complications such as the development of cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, or cholangiocarcinoma, as well as time to liver transplantation, measured from the date of PSC diagnosis. Secondary outcomes included characterization of triad phenotyping, defined as the simultaneous presence of PSC, CeD, and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which represents a distinct clinical entity with potentially unique pathophysiologic mechanisms. Additionally, the diagnostic sequence specifically, the temporal order in which PSC and CeD were diagnosed, was analyzed to determine whether one condition typically preceded the other and whether this sequence influenced clinical outcomes. These outcome metrics were selected to represent clinically meaningful endpoints relevant to patient care and to facilitate a comprehensive assessment of how coexisting celiac disease may influence the natural history, disease progression, and clinical management of PSC.

## Comparator Cohorts and Statistical Analysis

Two comparator cohorts were identified consecutively from the same registry, matched 3:1 on age at PSC diagnosis and gender, without pre-selecting for clinical course: patients with PSC and IBD but without CeD (PSC + IBD, n = 54), and patients with PSC alone (PSC-only, n = 54). Demographic, medication, ALP, and transplant data were extracted from structured EPIC fields and problem-list text; hepatic complications (cirrhosis, fibrosis, autoimmune hepatitis overlap, and portal hypertension-related complications including varices and ascites) were ascertained by manual chart review, consistent with the primary cohort.

Continuous variables (age, ALP) were compared across the three cohorts by one-way ANOVA or Kruskal- Wallis test, with pairwise comparisons by Student's t-test or Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables (sex, race, ethnicity, transplant, biologic use, ursodiol use, hepatic complications) were compared by chisquare test, with pairwise comparisons by Fisher's exact test. Normality of continuous variables was assessed with the Shapiro-Wilk test; ALP values departed significantly from a normal distribution in both matched comparator cohorts (p < 0.0001), so the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for all ALP comparisons. Given the exploratory nature of these pairwise comparisons across multiple outcomes and cohorts, p-values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons; results of individual pairwise tests should therefore be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Treatment-stratified subgroup counts (biologic and ursodiol exposure vs. transplant and cirrhosis, within each cohort) are reported descriptively only, without formal significance testing, given the small subgroup sizes involved. Two-tailed p < 0.05 was considered significant.

## Results

Among 7.5 million RPDR patients, 18,375 had celiac disease and 992 had PSC. Expected overlap by chance was 2.43 cases; 13 were observed in RPDR (OR 5.35, 95% CI 3.08–9.30; p < 0.001), indicating significantly increased co-occurrence. An additional 5 cases were identified from other data sources, bringing the total to 18 patients with dual PSC and celiac disease.

Baseline demographic characteristics and IBD distribution are summarized in (Table 1). The cohort included 12 males and 6 females, with a mean age of 47.8 years at PSC diagnosis and 44.4 years at celiac disease diagnosis. Most patients were White (94%) and non-Hispanic (89%). Concomitant inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) was present in 13 patients (72.2%), most commonly ulcerative colitis (10 patients, 55.6%), followed by Crohn’s disease (2 patients, 11.1%) and indeterminate colitis (1 patient, 5.6%). Among the two patients with Crohn’s disease, one had ileocolonic involvement and one had upper gastrointestinal involvement with ileal disease. Five patients (27.8%) had no documented IBD. Glutenfree diet adherence was documented in 16 patients (88.9%).

## Medication exposure

Medication exposure is summarized in (Table 2a). Ursodiol was the most commonly prescribed agent (55.6%), often continued for over a decade, consistent with standard PSC management. Mesalamine was used by 55.6% for UC control, frequently for ≥ 15 years. Tacrolimus (22.2%) and azathioprine (27.8%), as well as biologic agents including adalimumab, infliximab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, golimumab, and risankizumab, were used across the cohort. Escalation to biologic therapy (n = 7) occurred in patients with moderate to severe disease or treatment-refractory IBD.

Among the 14 non-transplanted patients, the mean PSC disease duration was approximately 8.8 years, with a range between 2 and 24 years. Approximately 79% of these non-transplanted patients adhered to a gluten-free diet. Cirrhosis was present in about 29% of this group, either before or during follow-up. Temporal Sequence of Diagnosis

The sequence of disease onset varied considerably (Fig. 1). Among the PSC + CeD cohort (n = 18), IBD was diagnosed first in 7 patients (38.9%), celiac disease (CeD) first in 7 patients (38.9%), and PSC first in 3 patients (16.7%); the order could not be determined in the remaining patient (5.6%).

Among the 7 patients with IBD first: IBD → CeD occurred in 4 (mean interval 4.8 years), of whom 3 went on to PSC (mean interval 2.9 years); IBD → PSC occurred in 3 (mean interval 4.4 years), all of whom went on to CeD (mean interval 4.7 years).

Among the 7 patients with CeD first: CeD → PSC occurred in 5 (mean interval 3.4 years), of whom 2 went on to IBD (mean interval 12.5 years); CeD → IBD occurred in 2 (mean interval 4.3 years), both of whom went on to PSC (mean interval 7.7 years).

Among the 3 patients with PSC first: PSC → CeD occurred in all 3 (mean interval 2.2 years), with 1 going on to IBD (interval 11.0 years). Disease Severity

Patients with coexisting PSC, celiac disease (CeD), and ulcerative colitis (UC) were followed longitudinally for variable durations. All patients with CeD had documented adherence to a gluten-free diet during follow-up.

Hepatobiliary complications, including hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension, recurrent cholangitis, and liver transplantation, were observed across the cohort (Table 3). Cirrhosis and advanced liver disease occurred in patients with both well-controlled and active intestinal disease states.

UC management included mesalamine maintenance therapy in most patients, with escalation to immunosuppressive or biologic agents in those with more extensive or refractory disease (Table 2a). Comparison with Matched PSC Control Cohorts

To contextualize these findings, the PSC + CeD cohort (± IBD; n = 18) was compared with two control cohorts drawn from the same registry and approximately matched on age at PSC diagnosis: patients with PSC and IBD but without celiac disease (PSC + IBD, n = 54) and patients with PSC alone (PSC-only, n = 54) (Table 1). Age at PSC diagnosis, sex, and ethnicity were broadly similar across the three cohorts. Mean follow-up from PSC diagnosis was 11.59 years (range 2.0–27.6) in the PSC + IBD controls and 8.46 years (range 0.02–18.44) in the PSC-only controls.

Liver transplantation was numerically more frequent in the PSC + CeD cohort (22.2%) than in PSC + IBD controls (5.6%) or PSC-only controls (13.0%), though this difference did not reach significance (chisquare p = 0.127) (Table 4, Fig. 3). Cirrhosis was likewise more common in the PSC + CeD cohort and in PSC-only controls than in PSC + IBD controls (50.0% and 51.9% vs 16.7%; chi-square p = 0.0002), fibrosis without cirrhosis was more common in the PSC + CeD and PSC + IBD cohorts than in PSC-only controls (16.7% and 18.5% vs 0%; p = 0.005), and PSC–autoimmune hepatitis overlap was most frequent in the PSC + CeD cohort, intermediate in PSC + IBD controls, and absent in PSC-only controls (22.2% vs 9.3% vs 0%; chi-square p = 0.005) (Table 3, Fig. 4). Any hepatic complication was numerically most common in the PSC + CeD cohort (88.9% vs 63.0% PSC + IBD and 61.1% PSC-only), though this difference did not reach significance (p = 0.083). Hepatic complications and cirrhosis in the two control cohorts were ascertained by manual chart review, consistent with the approach used for the PSC + CeD cohort (Tables 1–5b).

ALP levels differed significantly across the three cohorts at both the pre-diagnosis and post-diagnosis/1- year time points (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.0019 and p = 0.0087, respectively). Pre-diagnosis ALP was highest in PSC-only controls (mean 245.6 U/L, n = 43), followed by the PSC + CeD cohort (155.4 U/L, n = 3) and PSC + IBD controls (138.7 U/L, n = 24). Case-cohort ALP data remain more limited than the control cohorts and should be interpreted with caution (Table 5a, Fig. 2).

Biologic use was numerically similar across the three cohorts (38.9% PSC + CeD vs 37.0% PSC + IBD controls vs 22.2% PSC-only controls) and did not differ significantly (chi-square p = 0.183). Ursodiol use, by contrast, was significantly lower in the PSC + CeD cohort (55.6%) than in PSC + IBD controls (70.4%) and PSC-only controls (85.2%) (chi-square p = 0.028) (Table 2b).

Time from PSC diagnosis to cirrhosis diagnosis trended later in the PSC + CeD cohort (mean 3.67 years, n = 3) than in either control cohort, where cirrhosis was typically detected at or near the time of PSC diagnosis (PSC + IBD mean 0.87 years, n = 10; PSC-only mean − 0.08 years, n = 25; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.058) (Table 6, Fig. 5). Given the small case-cohort sample, this later apparent timing should be regarded as a preliminary signal rather than a confirmed finding.

## Discussion

This study provides one of the largest multi-institutional characterizations to date of patients with coexisting PSC, celiac disease, and ulcerative colitis. We found a significant enrichment of cooccurrence among these three immune-mediated disorders, well beyond what would be expected by chance, supporting a shared susceptibility rather than a coincidental clustering. Prior literature on this overlap has been limited to case reports and small series [2][4]; this analysis extends that work with outcome data from a more systematically identified cohort. That said, given the rarity of this combination and the retrospective, registry-based ascertainment, the magnitude of enrichment should be interpreted cautiously, as referral and detection bias likely inflate the apparent association to some degree.

Diagnostically, IBD and celiac disease were about equally likely to be the first condition identified, while PSC itself was rarely the presenting diagnosis, consistent with gastrointestinal or malabsorptive symptoms typically prompting workup before any hepatobiliary involvement is recognized. Notably, the interval between IBD and PSC diagnosis was far shorter in this cohort than in matched PSC + IBD controls, where IBD typically preceded PSC by over a decade, suggesting that celiac disease overlap may be associated with a more compressed, near-simultaneous multi-diagnosis presentation rather than the usual sequential pattern. Taken together with the known shared HLA-DR3/DQ2 susceptibility across these conditions, these findings support a pattern of immune-mediated clustering along the gut-liver axis [4][5].

With near-universal adherence to a gluten-free diet, liver-related morbidity remained substantial. Most patients developed at least one major hepatic complication, and roughly one in five required liver transplantation, at a burden at least as high as that reported in classical PSC cohorts [1]. This did not, however, translate into a clearly accelerated path to cirrhosis; if anything, cirrhosis tended to be identified later relative to PSC diagnosis than in either comparator cohort. Together, these observations suggest celiac disease overlap may be associated with a greater cumulative burden of hepatic complications and transplantation rather than a uniformly faster disease course, though this should be read as a

Page 13/21


<!-- Page 14 -->


preliminary signal given the small sample, potential referral bias, and the very limited number of patients with dateable cirrhosis onset in this cohort.

Benchmarking against the matched comparator cohorts helps localize where this excess burden concentrates. Liver transplantation and cirrhosis were both more common in the PSC + CeD cohort than in PSC + IBD controls, but cirrhosis rates in the PSC + CeD cohort closely resembled those in PSC-only controls, who also lack IBD. This raises the possibility that the presence of IBD itself may track with a comparatively milder hepatic course in PSC, and that the elevated hepatic burden seen with celiac overlap could partly reflect the absence of IBD rather than a specific effect of celiac disease, a distinction that will require larger, prospectively matched cohorts to resolve. The markedly higher rate of PSC-autoimmune hepatitis overlap in the PSC + CeD cohort, by contrast, does point toward a more specific link between celiac disease and overlapping autoimmune liver injury, consistent with the shared HLA-DR3/DQ2 susceptibility noted above.

In contrast to prior reports suggesting gluten-free diet improves gastrointestinal symptoms without meaningfully altering hepatic outcomes [9], our study offers a more comprehensive view of disease trajectory, incorporating diagnostic sequence and treatment exposure. Given the small number of transplanted patients with celiac disease in this cohort, no firm conclusions can be drawn about posttransplant course. Anecdotally, none developed recurrent PSC during follow-up, though this observation is far too limited to support any inference about whether GFD adherence modifies post-transplant recurrence risk, a phenomenon reported in a meaningful minority of transplanted PSC patients without celiac disease, and one that remains a worthwhile question for future prospective study [7][8].

The sequence of diagnoses was notably heterogeneous, with no single trajectory clearly dominant across the cohort; patients arrived at this triad by varied and sometimes closely spaced pathways rather than a single classical progression. This underscores the need for vigilant cross-screening: persistent gastrointestinal or nutritional symptoms in PSC or IBD should prompt evaluation for celiac disease [2][5], while abnormal liver biochemistry or bowel symptoms in celiac disease warrant hepatobiliary and colonic assessment [1].

Mechanistically, our findings support the hypothesis that shared immune pathways, potentially mediated through common HLA-associated antigen presentation, underlie this disease constellation [4][5]. Clinical trajectories, however, still appeared largely driven by the dominant condition: PSC shaping hepatic outcomes [1], celiac disease shaping malabsorption [3], and UC shaping colonic inflammation, with limited evidence that treating one condition consistently altered the course of the others. This reinforces the need for individualized, multidisciplinary management rather than assuming a single unifying disease course.

Clinically, these findings suggest a need for heightened awareness of occult celiac disease in PSC patients, particularly those with UC, and reciprocal awareness of PSC in celiac patients with abnormal liver tests [2][5]. While gluten-free diet adherence was associated with improvement in celiac-related symptoms, it did not appear to alter PSC progression in most cases [9]. The absence of post-transplant

Page 14/21


<!-- Page 15 -->


recurrence among transplanted patients in this cohort is worth noting but, given the small numbers and limited follow-up, should be interpreted cautiously and requires validation in larger studies [7][8].

The strengths of this study include its multi-institutional design, rigorous diagnostic confirmation, and extended follow-up; incorporating matched PSC + IBD and PSC-only control cohorts also addressed the lack of a comparator group inherent to the primary cohort alone. Limitations are nonetheless substantial: treatment-stratified subgroups were too small to support formal statistical comparison and are reported descriptively only, gluten-free diet adherence could not be tested against outcomes because no clearly non-adherent patients were identified for comparison, and the retrospective, modest-sized primary cohort remains susceptible to referral and documentation bias. Genotypic and environmental exposure data were also incomplete. These limitations temper generalizability, and larger, prospective, populationbased studies incorporating immunophenotyping and environmental exposures are needed to confirm and extend these findings.

In conclusion, this study provides further evidence for a clinically significant overlap between PSC, celiac disease, and UC. The high burden of hepatic complications observed, alongside the absence of posttransplant recurrence in GFD-adherent patients, underscores both the clinical significance of this association and the need for further mechanistic and therapeutic investigation [1][5]. These findings support integrated, multidisciplinary care and provide a framework for future work exploring gut-liver immune interactions in autoimmune disease.

## Abstract

Background: Fatigue and pruritus are common and disabling in primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), but their severity is not reliably explained by standard biochemical markers. Whether liver stiffness measured by transient elastography reflects these symptoms remains unclear. This study examined associations between liver stiffness and fatigue and pruritus in PBC and PSC, and between routine biochemical measures and symptom burden. Methods: This cross-sectional analysis included 107 patients (56 PBC, 51 PSC) from a prospective autoimmune liver disease registry. Fatigue was assessed with the CLDQ-29 fatigue domain and pruritus with the CLDQ-29 pruritus item or the itch visual analog scale. Multivariable linear and ordered logistic regression examined associations between liver stiffness and fatigue and pruritus, adjusted for disease type, age, and sex. Spearman correlations assessed associations between liver stiffness and clinical and laboratory variables, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Receiver operating characteristic analysis assessed discrimination. Results: Patients with PBC were older (59 vs. 51 years; p < 0.001) and more often female (96.4% vs. 56.9%; p < 0.001) than those with PSC. Liver stiffness (6.0 vs. 6.8 kPa; p = 0.101), fatigue scores, pruritus scores, and itch VAS were similar between groups. Liver stiffness was not associated with fatigue (β = 0.005; p = 0.835) or pruritus (OR = 0.97; p = 0.190) after adjustment; only age was associated with fatigue (β = 0.021; p = 0.020). Among laboratory measures, only ALP remained correlated with liver stiffness after correction (ρ = 0.309; adjusted p = 0.027). In PSC alone, higher liver stiffness was associated with worse pruritus (ρ = −0.37; p = 0.009), a finding not seen in PBC. Liver stiffness alone showed limited discrimination for fatigue (AUC 0.46) and pruritus (AUC 0.56); a model with disease type, age, and sex improved discrimination modestly for fatigue (AUC 0.60) but not for pruritus (AUC 0.57). Conclusions: Liver stiffness was not associated with fatigue or pruritus in the overall cohort of patients with PBC and PSC, and a possible association with pruritus in PSC needs confirmation. Patient-reported outcomes should be assessed alongside biochemical and elastographic measures, and how they relate to objective measures of disease remains an open question.

## 1. Introduction

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) are chronic autoimmune liver diseases characterized by cholestasis, but differ substantially in clinical course and management [1,2,3,4]. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) remains the standard first-line therapy for PBC, with second-line agents available for the 30–40% of patients who do not achieve an adequate biochemical response, while no therapy has been proven to slow disease progression in PSC, where management focuses on surveillance, treatment of complications, and timely referral for liver transplantation [5,6,7,8,9]. Despite having different management and treatment algorithms, fatigue and pruritus are frequently described among the most disabling symptoms, and have a major impact on quality of life [10,11,12]. A prospective analysis of 1267 patients found fatigue to be frequent in both PBC and PSC, particularly among women [13]. Notably, the severity of these symptoms is not reliably explained by disease stage or standard biochemical markers of cholestasis, particularly in PBC [14,15].

Liver stiffness measurement by vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) is a simple, non-invasive tool used to stage liver fibrosis in autoimmune liver diseases, including PBC and PSC [16]. Prior work linking elastography to disease outcomes in PBC and PSC has largely focused on clinical course and prognosis rather than patient-reported outcomes [17,18]. Studies of fatigue and pruritus in these diseases have typically examined biochemical and clinical correlates, such as ALP, GGT, and cirrhosis [13]. To our knowledge, no study has evaluated the elastography–symptom relationship for both fatigue and pruritus, in both PBC and PSC, within the same cohort.

In this study, the primary aim was to examine associations between liver stiffness measured by transient elastography and fatigue and pruritus in PBC and PSC. Secondary analyses evaluated associations between routine biochemical measures and symptom burden.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Study Design and Population

This cross-sectional study used data from the prospective Autoimmune Liver Disease Registry at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), which enrolled patients from January 2018 through November 2025. Participants completed questionnaires during routine clinic visits. We retrieved clinical information, laboratory results, and transient elastography measurements from the study REDCap database.

Adult patients with PBC or PSC were eligible. Diagnoses were based on accepted clinical practice guidelines [19,20] and verified by chart review. Patients with overlap syndromes, including those whose diagnosis evolved during follow-up, and those with other autoimmune liver diseases were not included. This allowed the PBC and PSC groups to be examined separately.

The enrollment visit served as the index visit. Participants needed complete Chronic Liver Disease Questionnaire (CLDQ)-29 responses for the fatigue score and pruritus assessment, as well as laboratory values and a valid transient elastography result obtained within six months of enrollment. Patients meeting these criteria were included in the analytic cohort. Figure 1 shows the flowchart for patient selection.

### 2.2. Patient-Reported Outcomes

The CLDQ-29 was administered at enrollment by clinicians or research staff. It assesses symptoms during the prior 2 weeks on a 1–7 scale. Fatigue-domain scores were calculated as the mean of the relevant items, with higher scores indicating better health-related quality of life.

Pruritus was assessed using either the CLDQ-29 pruritus item or the 0–10 itch visual analog scale (VAS), depending on the available response. A positive pruritus variable was defined by reported itching on either measure, allowing inclusion of patients who completed only one pruritus assessment. Higher VAS scores indicated worse itching, whereas lower CLDQ-29 pruritus-item scores indicated greater symptom burden.

### 2.3. Clinical Data, Study Variables, and Outcomes

Baseline variables included age, sex, race and ethnicity, body mass index (BMI), disease duration, alcohol use, smoking history, cirrhosis, portal hypertension-related findings, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), sleep difficulty, depression, anxiety, and medication use. Cirrhosis was based on documented findings from abdominal ultrasound (US) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). For patients with PSC, the presence of IBD was recorded when available.

Laboratory measures included aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), total bilirubin, albumin, platelet count, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), international normalized ratio (INR), creatinine, sodium, white blood cell count (WBC), vitamin D level, Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, and Child-Pugh score when available. Medication variables included ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), fibrates, vitamin D supplementation, and pruritus-directed therapies.

Liver stiffness was measured by vibration-controlled transient elastography and reported in kilopascals (kPa). When clinically indicated, examinations were performed by one of two trained technicians. Technicians knew the clinical indication but did not have access to registry questionnaire responses. Patients fasted for at least 3 h before testing. Measurements were obtained from standardized intercostal spaces to identify the lowest valid liver stiffness value. Each examination included at least 10 valid measurements. Reliable examinations required an interquartile range-to-median ratio of 30% or less. Propagation maps were reviewed for parallel shear-wave margins and fewer than two incorrect shear-wave maps caused by rib echoes [21].

The primary outcome was to examine the association between liver stiffness and fatigue or pruritus. Secondary analyses evaluated the relationships of routine biochemical measures with these PRO and with liver stiffness.

### 2.4. Statistical Analysis

Baseline characteristics are summarized by disease phenotype. Continuous variables are presented as median and interquartile range (IQR), and categorical variables as number and percentage. PBC and PSC were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and Fisher exact test for categorical variables. No formal sample size calculation was performed because the analysis included all eligible registry participants with data available for the cross-sectional study. The sample therefore reflects the available clinical registry cohort during the study period.

Multivariable linear regression was used to examine the association between liver stiffness and the CLDQ-29 fatigue-domain score. Ordered logistic regression was used for the CLDQ-29 pruritus item. Both models included liver stiffness, disease phenotype, age, and sex. These covariates were selected based on their clinical relevance and consistent availability across the PBC and PSC groups. Other clinical variables were not included as adjustment covariates because they were disease-specific, incompletely available, or evaluated separately as secondary clinical measures. The model was limited to clinically relevant covariates to avoid overfitting given the sample size. Linear-regression results are reported as regression coefficients (β) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and ordered logistic-regression results as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs. Adjusted R2 and McFadden pseudo-R2 were reported for the fatigue and pruritus models, respectively.

Spearman rank correlations assessed unadjusted associations between liver stiffness and clinical variables, laboratory measures, fatigue, pruritus, and itch visual analog scale (VAS) scores in the overall cohort. Correlations between liver stiffness and fatigue or pruritus were also examined separately in PBC and PSC. For the overall correlation analysis, p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses assessed the ability of liver stiffness alone and the multivariable model to discriminate fatigue impairment and pruritus burden. For the ROC analyses, fatigue impairment was operationally defined as a CLDQ-29 fatigue-domain score < 5, based on previous work using a score of 5 to distinguish lower from higher health-related quality of life and on the interpretation of the CLDQ response scale [22,23]. Pruritus burden was defined as an itch VAS score ≥ 4 on the 0–10 scale, consistent with previously proposed thresholds for at least moderate pruritus [24]. The multivariable model included liver stiffness, disease phenotype, age, and sex. Areas under the ROC curve (AUCs) are reported with 95% CIs.

Analyses used complete observations for each comparison; sample sizes therefore varied according to data availability. No imputation was performed. Analyses were conducted in Stata version 19.5 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). Python version 3.11 was used for data visualization. All tests were two-sided, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

### 2.5. Ethical Considerations

The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the principles of Good Clinical Practice. The BIDMC Institutional Review Board (IRB) approved the study under protocol 2018P00019, with approval valid through 9 December 2026. All participants provided written informed consent.

## 3. Results

### 3.1. Baseline Characteristics of the Study Cohort

The cohort included 107 patients, 56 with PBC and 51 with PSC (Table 1). Patients with PBC were older than those with PSC (median age, 59 vs. 51 years; p < 0.001) and were more often female (96.4% vs. 56.9%; p < 0.001). IBD was present in 52.9% of patients with PSC and in none with PBC (p < 0.001). Anxiety symptoms were also more common in PSC (33.3% vs. 10.7%; p = 0.005). Liver stiffness was similar between groups (6.0 vs. 6.8 kPa; p = 0.101). Fatigue scores, pruritus scores, and itch VAS were also similar between PBC and PSC, with no significant differences observed.

### 3.2. Factors Associated with Fatigue and Pruritus

In the multivariable analysis, liver stiffness was not associated with fatigue after adjustment for disease type, age, and sex (β = 0.005, 95% CI −0.038 to 0.047; p = 0.835) (Table 2). Age was associated with fatigue, with higher scores observed in older patients (β = 0.021, 95% CI 0.003–0.039; p = 0.020). Disease type and sex were not associated with fatigue. For pruritus, liver stiffness was also not associated with greater symptom severity (OR = 0.97, 95% CI 0.92–1.02; p = 0.190), and disease type, age, and sex were not significantly associated.

### 3.3. Associations Between Liver Stiffness, Clinical Variables, and PRO

In the overall cohort, ALP was the only variable that remained significantly associated with liver stiffness after Benjamini–Hochberg correction (ρ = 0.309, adjusted p = 0.027). Albumin and Child-Pugh score were related to liver stiffness in the unadjusted analysis, although these findings did not persist after correction. No clear correlation was seen for bilirubin, AST, ALT, MELD score, platelet count, BMI, or vitamin D level. Fatigue and pruritus also showed no meaningful relationship with liver stiffness when all patients were considered together (Table 3).

Figure 2 shows the disease-specific relationships between liver stiffness and PROs. Fatigue was not correlated with liver stiffness in either PBC or PSC, and pruritus was also unrelated to liver stiffness in PBC. In PSC, however, higher liver stiffness was associated with lower pruritus-item scores (ρ = −0.37, p = 0.009). Because lower scores indicate worse pruritus, this corresponded to greater pruritus severity at higher liver stiffness values. Figure 2 also shows substantial variation in symptom scores across the range of liver stiffness, particularly for fatigue.

### 3.4. Discriminatory Performance of Liver Stiffness for Fatigue and Pruritus

Figure 3 shows the ROC curve analyses for fatigue and pruritus. Liver stiffness alone had little discriminatory value for either outcome, with estimates of 0.46 (95% CI 0.35–0.57) for fatigue and 0.56 (95% CI 0.45–0.69) for pruritus. The full clinical model improved discrimination for fatigue to 0.60 (95% CI 0.48–0.70), but the estimate for pruritus remained essentially unchanged at 0.57 (95% CI 0.45–0.68). Overall, the models showed limited ability to distinguish patients according to fatigue or pruritus burden.

## 4. Discussion

In this cross-sectional analysis of patients with PBC and PSC, we found that liver stiffness was not associated with fatigue or pruritus after adjustment for disease type, age, and sex. Fatigue was also unrelated to liver stiffness within each disease, and so was pruritus in PBC. Interestingly, in PSC alone, higher liver stiffness was associated with worse pruritus in an unadjusted analysis. Among the laboratory measures, only ALP correlated with liver stiffness after correction.

Previous reports are consistent with these results, suggesting that symptoms in PBC and PSC do not clearly correlate with disease stage, which may be why they were not related to liver stiffness. In PBC, symptom burden shows no noteworthy correlation with the stage of liver disease [15]. In PSC, a recent study found no association between transient elastography and quality of life [25], although an Australian cohort linked patient-reported outcomes to disease severity, mainly decompensated cirrhosis and cholangitis [26]. Cirrhosis and advanced liver disease have been associated with worse quality of life and fatigue [27], but liver stiffness was low in our cohort and cirrhosis was uncommon (Table 1). ALP was the only laboratory measure associated with liver stiffness.

Fatigue in cholestatic disease is multifactorial, and its pathophysiology remains largely unknown [14,27]. It appears to rely on factors that stiffness does not capture. Kruk et al. linked it to ALP, GGT, and cirrhosis [13], and hypothyroidism, anemia, and depression are recognized contributors in PBC [15]. In our cohort, age was the only variable associated with fatigue. Other recognized contributors, such as IBD, anxiety symptoms, and sleep difficulty, were present in our patients (Table 1) but were not included in the models, and hemoglobin, iron, vitamin B12, folate, thyroid function, and extrahepatic autoimmune diseases were not available. Sleep disorders have been associated with greater fatigue in PBC [28].

Regarding pruritus, in PBC it was unrelated to liver stiffness, consistent with reports that pruritus severity does not always correlate with symptoms in this disease [29], and to our knowledge this relationship has not been examined before. In PSC, higher liver stiffness was associated with worse pruritus in an unadjusted, exploratory analysis; a similar pattern was reported by Hussain et al., who found greater itch intensity in patients with PSC and higher transient elastography values [30]. Pruritus also has causes that stiffness does not measure: bile acids, lysophosphatidic acid, autotaxin, and the bile acid receptor MRGPRX4 are thought to contribute, and IL-31 levels correlate with itch scores in both PSC and PBC [31,32,33].

Overall, liver stiffness did not reflect patient-reported symptom burden in our cohort, although the possible link with pruritus in PSC warrants confirmation. Patient-reported outcomes such as the CLDQ and Itch VAS should therefore be collected alongside biochemical and elastographic measures [34,35].

This study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional design does not allow conclusions regarding causality. Second, it was a single-center study, and no formal sample size calculation was performed because all eligible registry participants were included. Third, our models adjusted only for disease type, age, and sex. Other potential confounders, including IBD, sleep difficulty, depression, and anxiety, were not included as covariates. Pruritus-directed medication and psychiatric conditions were also excluded, as too few patients had these to model reliably. Residual confounding is possible from IBD activity, thyroid dysfunction, other autoimmune or systemic disorders, anemia, and nutritional deficiencies, since hemoglobin, iron, vitamin B12, folate, thyroid function, and extrahepatic autoimmune diseases were not among the study variables. Fourth, the disease-specific correlations, including the PSC pruritus finding, are unadjusted for multiple comparisons, and the proportional odds assumption was not formally tested. Finally, questionnaires were completed at enrollment, whereas elastography and laboratory values were allowed within six months, so assessments were not simultaneous, and elastography was performed by technicians who knew the clinical indication, although reliability criteria were applied.

Future studies should be longitudinal and multicenter, with a common time window for elastography, laboratory tests, and questionnaires, and should record hemoglobin, iron, vitamin B12, folate, thyroid function, and IBD activity. They should add psychological measures as in SOMA.LIV [36], the CLDQ-PBC [37], and CLDQ-PSC [38], and IL-31 [33] as a pruritogen biomarker. New study endpoints are needed to correlate patient-reported outcomes with objective measures of disease.

## 5. Conclusions

In this cross-sectional study, liver stiffness was not associated with fatigue or pruritus in the overall cohort of patients with PBC and PSC, and a possible association with pruritus in PSC needs confirmation. These findings describe associations and do not establish causal relationships. Patient-reported outcomes should be assessed alongside biochemical and elastographic measures, and how they relate to objective measures of disease remains a major open question that requires new study endpoints.

## Abstract

Background: The Mayo Risk Score (MRS) predicts short-term mortality in primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) using the age, bilirubin, albumin, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and variceal bleeding history. While the MRS has been validated in end-stage PSC, its ability to predict liver transplantation (LT) and outcomes in newly diagnosed patients without advanced disease remains unclear. This study evaluated the effectiveness of the MRS in predicting LT and mortality in this patient population. Methods: We analyzed data from 109 adults with PSC enrolled in a prospective registry (2018–2024) with ≥4 years of follow-up. Logistic regression identified the predictors of LT or death, and the model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Multicollinearity was evaluated using the variance inflation factor (VIF). Results: Among the 109 patients (mean age 45 ± 15 years, 51% female), 85% remained alive without LT, 12% underwent LT, and 3% died over a median follow-up of 4.63 years. The MRS was significantly associated with LT or death (OR 3.08, p < 0.001) and demonstrated excellent predictive performance (AUROC 0.99, p < 0.001). The model achieved 95.45% sensitivity, 98.85% specificity, and a correct classification rate of 98.17%, supporting its clinical utility. Conclusion: The MRS is a robust tool for risk stratification in PSC, predicting LT and mortality. These findings highlight its broader applicability beyond end-stage PSC and underscore its potential for guiding clinical management and early intervention strategies.

## 1. Introduction

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts [1]. The clinical course of PSC is highly heterogeneous, with severe cases progressing to cirrhosis, liver failure, and an elevated risk of malignancies [2]. Notably, patients with PSC, particularly those with concomitant inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), face an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer [2,3]. Studies from tertiary referral centers estimate a median transplant-free survival of 15 to 21 years following a PSC diagnosis, although this may be longer in population-based settings [4,5]. Currently, no treatment for PSC has been demonstrated to prevent disease progression [6].

The prevalence of PSC in North America and Europe ranges from 6 to 16 cases per 100,000 individuals, with population-based studies in North America estimating an incidence of approximately 1 case per 100,000 persons [1,7,8]. Although rare, PSC poses a substantial healthcare burden due to the lack of effective therapies and its status as a major indication for liver transplantation (LT) [9]. LT is the only established treatment shown to improve survival in PSC patients with end-stage liver disease (ESLD) [10]. Among the autoimmune liver diseases (AILDs) [11], PSC is now the leading indication for LT and ranks as the fifth most common indication for LT overall in the United States [12,13].

In this context, risk prediction models are crucial to estimating prognosis and evaluating the likelihood of future events in patients with PSC. Among these models, the Mayo Risk Score (MRS) is the most widely utilized tool for estimating the short-term (4-year) mortality risk in PSC patients [14]. However, the MRS has several notable limitations, including the variability in some of its parameters, which are prone to fluctuation, and its inability to reliably predict long-term outcomes [15]. Furthermore, since the MRS was developed in a tertiary transplant center in the United States, its use has been largely restricted to patients with ESLD. In a validation and risk stratification study by Goode et al., the MRS demonstrated prognostic value for predicting the two-year outcomes in a cohort of 1001 patients, which ultimately led to the proposal of the United Kingdom-PSC (UK-PSC) score as an alternative [16].

More recently, intensive efforts have been devoted to improving prognostic modeling. While these efforts have advanced the field, distinguishing factors associated with early, rapidly progressing disease from those indicative of advanced stages remains a critical challenge [17]. A systematic review by Schmeltzer et al. compared the revised MRS with three other prognostic models: the Amsterdam–Oxford Model (AOM), the UK-PSC, and the PSC Risk Estimate Tool (PREsTo). The revised MRS outperformed the AOM in c-statistics but did not meet the 0.8 threshold indicative of strong prognostic models. In contrast, with a 10-year time horizon, the UK-PSC model achieved a c-statistic exceeding 0.8. Similarly, the PREsTo model, developed using machine learning, surpassed this threshold. Unlike the revised MRS, the PREsTo model excluded advanced PSC cases and focused on hepatic decompensation as its primary endpoint [18].

Prognostic models are essential in managing PSC, helping guide patient counseling concerning disease progression, optimizing selection for LT, and stratifying participants in clinical trials of novel therapies. Ensuring these models demonstrate transferability and can be confidently applied across diverse PSC patient populations is critical. Therefore, we aimed to further validate the MRS and assess its utility in a prospective cohort of patients in the U.S. This study is the first to validate the MRS as a predictor of LT and mortality in patients with recently diagnosed PSC who do not yet show signs of advanced disease, addressing a crucial gap in its clinical application.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Study Population

Participants for this study were selected from a prospective autoimmune liver disease registry at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC; Boston, MA, USA). The registry enrollment period spanned from January 2018 to November 2024. Complete follow-up was defined as LT, death, or clinical follow-up extending beyond four years. Patients who were diagnosed with PSC at the age of 18 or older, according to accepted diagnostic criteria and standards of care, were included (Figure 1).

In the early stages, PSC is often characterized by asymptomatic serum liver enzyme abnormalities, while signs of cirrhosis appear later. We established exclusion criteria to reflect cases without advanced disease, as clear clinical criteria for early-stage PSC remain challenging. To ensure this, we excluded individuals who met any of the following criteria: (a) aged under 18, (b) presence of another concurrent liver disease, (c) lack of available laboratory results, (d) cholangiocarcinoma at baseline, (e) a MELD score above 14, (f) history of liver transplantation, (g) evidence of portal hypertension at baseline, defined as the presence of varices, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, splenomegaly, or a platelet count below 150 × 10⁹/L, (h) histologic stage 3 fibrosis, characterized by areas of fibrosis connecting to each other, or stage 4 fibrosis, marked by widespread, honeycomb-like scarring (cirrhosis), and (i) missing data required for score assessment. Ultimately, we evaluated 109 adult patients who met the cohort criteria, ensuring the selection of cases without advanced disease.

### 2.2. Study Outcomes, Variables, and Definitions

The primary outcome of this study was to assess the predictive accuracy of the MRS for LT and mortality in patients with recently diagnosed PSC who have not yet developed advanced disease. Patients were classified into three risk categories: low risk (R < 0), intermediate risk (0 ≤ R < 2), and high risk (R ≥ 2). The predicted score for each patient was calculated at baseline according to the revised MRS [14]. The MRS was determined using the following formula:MRS = 0.03 × [age (years)] + 0.54 × In [bilirubin (mg/dL)] × In [AST (U/L)] − 0.84 × [albumin (g/dL)] + 1.24 (if a history of variceal bleeding was present)(1)

### 2.3. Statistical Analysis

Demographic, clinical, and biochemical markers were collected. Normally distributed data are reported as the mean and standard deviation (SD), while skewed data are summarized as the median and interquartile range (IQR). Continuous variable distributions were visualized using boxplots, and group comparisons were performed with t-tests or Mann–Whitney U tests, as appropriate. Categorical variables, expressed as percentages, were compared using Pearson’s chi-squared test (χ2).

Logistic regression models were used to assess factors associated with the risk of transplantation or death at diagnosis. The univariate analysis included clinically relevant variables not inherently part of the MRS estimation, including gender, presence of IBD, bile duct involvement, ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) treatment, and laboratory results for alkaline phosphatase (ALP), platelet count (PL), and the value of the MRS. The results are reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The multivariate model was constructed using stepwise logistic regression to identify the most significant independent predictors. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Multicollinearity among the predictors in the multivariable model was assessed using the variance inflation factor (VIF).

The model’s predictive performance was evaluated by calculating and plotting the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and estimating the corresponding 95% CI. Similarly, we assessed the clinical performance of the MRS by calculating the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) to determine its ability to identify patients at high risk of transplant or death in PSC without advanced disease.

All the statistical analyses were conducted using Stata version 18.0 (StataCorp LP, College Station, TX, USA).

## 3. Results

### 3.1. Baseline Characteristics

The baseline characteristics of the cohort (n = 109) revealed a mean age at diagnosis of 45 years (SD 15), with a slight female predominance (51%). The majority of patients were White (79%), followed by African American (9%) and Hispanic (6%) patients. Concomitant IBD was present in 57% of patients, predominantly ulcerative colitis (UC) (45%), with Crohn’s disease (CD) observed in 11%. Large duct involvement was identified in 51% of patients, while small duct involvement was present in 26%. UDCA treatment was used by 57% of the cohort, with a median dose of 13 mg/kg/day. The laboratory values at diagnosis showed elevated ALP levels (median 154 IU/L, IQR 100–301) and normal TBIL levels (median 0.5 mg/dL, IQR 0.4–0.8).

The cohort was followed for a median of 4.63 years (SD 3.58), during which 85% of patients remained alive without LT, 12% underwent LT, and 3% died. The median MRS was −0.5 (IQR −1.03 to −0.02), with 80% classified as low risk (MRS < 0), 18% as intermediate risk (0 ≤ MRS < 2), and 3% as high risk (MRS ≥ 2). These findings highlight the predominance of low-risk patients at baseline, although a subset progressed to severe outcomes. The baseline characteristics of the cohort are detailed in Table 1.

### 3.2. Risk Classification

Patients were classified into the low-risk (n = 87), intermediate-risk (n = 19), and high-risk (n = 3) groups based on the MRS (Table 2). Concomitant IBD was observed in 45% of low-risk, 53% of intermediate-risk, and 33% of high-risk patients (p = 0.873). Notably, large duct involvement was more frequent in the intermediate-risk group (68%) compared to the low-risk (47%) and high-risk (33%) groups; however, this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.177).

The laboratory markers at diagnosis varied significantly between the groups, with ALP (p = 0.010), AST (p = 0.003), ALT (p = 0.028), and TBIL (p < 0.001) all being higher in the high-risk group. At the same time, ALB was significantly lower (p < 0.001) in this group. The median follow-up duration was significantly shorter in the high-risk group (2.72 years) compared to the low- and intermediate-risk groups (5 years; p < 0.001).

The outcomes at follow-up showed that all the high-risk patients either underwent LT (33%) or died (66%), while 91% of the low-risk and 74% of intermediate-risk patients remained alive without LT (p < 0.001). The MRS increased progressively from the low- to high-risk groups (−0.8, 0.64, and 2.03, respectively; p < 0.001)

The univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses identified key factors associated with the risk of LT or death in patients diagnosed with PSC (Table 3). In the univariate analysis, the significant predictors included the PL (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.98–0.99, p = 0.031) and MRS (OR 3.00, 95% CI 1.71–5.60, p < 0.001) values. Additionally, the pseudo-R2 values indicate that the MRS (0.178) had the strongest association with transplantation or death, followed by the PL value (0.111), while the ALP value (0.013) contributed minimally to the model. Multivariate analysis confirmed that the MRS (OR 3.08, 95% CI 1.71–5.58, p < 0.001) was an independent predictor of adverse outcomes.

Furthermore, a multicollinearity assessment of the predictors revealed a mean VIF of 1.17, with individual values ranging from 1.05 to 1.33. This indicates no significant collinearity among the included variables. Supplementary Table S1 provides further details.

Figure 2 illustrates the distribution of the MRSs across the three outcome categories: alive without LT, undergoing LT, and death. Patients who remained alive without undergoing LT had the lowest MRSs, with a median score below zero and a few outliers with higher values. In contrast, patients who underwent LT exhibited elevated MRS values. The highest scores were observed in patients who died, with minimal variability within this group. These findings suggest that elevated MRS values are strongly associated with adverse outcomes, including the need for LT and mortality.

### 3.3. Predictive Performance

We confirmed the high discriminatory power of the MRS in predicting the risk of LT and liver-related death in patients with PSC, achieving an AUROC of 0.99 (p < 0.001) (Figure 3).

The MRS demonstrated high predictive performance in identifying PSC patients at risk of transplant or death. With a sensitivity of 95.45% and a specificity of 98.85%, the score effectively distinguishes high-risk patients while minimizing false positives. The PPV (95.45%) and NPV (98.85%) underscore its clinical utility in accurately stratifying patients based on prognosis. The overall correct classification rate of 98.17% further supports the significant predictive accuracy of the MRS in this PSC cohort (Table 4).

## 4. Discussion

Our study demonstrates that the revised MRS is a reliable tool for predicting LT and mortality in patients with PSC. Wiesner et al. (1989) introduced the Natural History Model for PSC based on a cohort of 174 Mayo Clinic patients, identifying age, serum bilirubin, hemoglobin levels, IBD status, and histologic stage on liver biopsy as independent predictors of survival [19]. This model effectively stratified patients into the low-, moderate-, and high-risk groups. Kim et al. (2000) [14] subsequently proposed and validated the revised MRS, emphasizing its utility for risk stratification in advanced PSC [20]. Our findings build upon this work by confirming the MRS’s strong predictive performance in PSC patients without signs of advanced disease, highlighting its potential to guide clinical management before significant disease progression.

The validity of a prognostic model is best assessed in an independent yet comparable cohort. Using a prospective cohort of PSC patients enrolled at diagnosis, our study predominantly included low-risk patients based on the MRS classification. Over a five-year follow-up period, most patients survived without LT, while a subset required LT or died. The significant predictors of LT or death included a higher MRS, a severe MRS classification, and a lower ALB level, all confirmed by multivariate analysis. The MRS distribution aligned with the outcomes, with the lowest MRS among patients who survived without LT, intermediate values in those undergoing LT, and the highest in those who died. The model demonstrated excellent predictive performance (AUROC 0.99), surpassing prior studies reporting AUROCs of 0.63–0.85 [21].

The clinical impact of a recent PSC diagnosis as a predictor of LT and mortality in our study differed notably from the original MRS study, which used the date of referral rather than that of diagnosis as the starting point [14]. The MRS estimates the time to all-cause mortality but does not account for the time to LT, and for LT recipients, survival projections are based on the estimated life expectancy without LT [14]. A study by Tischendorf et al. analyzed 273 German PSC patients over a median follow-up of 76 months and found that the median survival rates based on death or LT as endpoints might be underestimated due to a high proportion (40%) undergoing LT, reflecting the hospital’s role as a leading LT center and advancements in LT techniques during 1990–2004 [21]. Similarly, Kim et al. compared the Child–Pugh classification and MRS in assessing PSC survival, noting that among 173 patients in the original MRS model, 147 had sufficient data for Child–Pugh scoring. Their findings highlighted the MRS’s superior utility in patients with less advanced disease, making it particularly valuable in clinical trials, where participants often have well-compensated liver function [22].

The MRS does not account for the variability in ALP levels, a key biochemical marker in PSC. Our study showed significantly higher baseline ALP levels in the high-risk group (p = 0.010). Elevated ALP, often accompanied by AST and ALT levels elevated to 2–3 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), is a hallmark of PSC and is frequently used as an endpoint in drug trials despite its predictive limitations [23]. A study by de Vries involving 366 PSC patients demonstrated the prognostic value of ALP levels, both at diagnosis and one year post-diagnosis, identifying an optimal one-year threshold of 1.3 times ULN. Notably, the one-year ALP levels were more predictive of outcomes such as LT and PSC-related deaths than the baseline levels [24]. These findings highlight the importance of developing prognostic models that integrate additional biochemical variables, particularly during follow-up, to improve the assessment of disease progression.

In addition, the ALB levels are part of the assessment of the MRS, which indicates their importance in evaluating disease severity and prognosis. However, the limited sensitivity of ALB in detecting mild or non-advanced disease reduces its effectiveness in such instances [25]. Moreover, lower pre-transplant albumin levels in patients with PSC have consistently been associated with poorer post-transplant outcomes [21,25]. Conversely, TBIL, like albumin, is included in the MRS, and elevated bilirubin remains a well-established predictor of a worse prognosis and a key component of several validated clinical predictive scores [14,19,25,26,27].

Our study found no significant differences in outcomes based on gender or concomitant IBD. While some evidence suggests that female sex and Crohn’s disease may be associated with a more favorable prognosis in PSC, this has been supported by multiple studies. A large observational study involving 44 hospitals across a geographically defined region in the Netherlands provided some of the strongest evidence for this association [4]. However, the impact of IBD on survival remains unclear, with inconsistent findings reported in the literature [28,29]. Our sample size of 109 patients was likely underpowered to detect such associations. Future studies with larger, well-adjusted cohorts are necessary to validate these findings, with a focus on the accurate classification of PSC-associated IBD and its correlation with risk stratification.

The clinical implications of our findings are significant. Early identification of high-risk patients through the MRS can inform closer monitoring, timely LT referral, and prioritization for inclusion in clinical trials. This aligns with observations by Trivedi et al., who emphasized the importance of early risk stratification in optimizing outcomes and resource allocation for PSC patients [4]. Moreover, identifying low-risk patients who are unlikely to experience rapid disease progression could reduce unnecessary interventions, alleviating healthcare costs and patient burdens.

This study’s prospective design has notable limitations, primarily due to its small cohort size. Due to the rarity of the disease, it is challenging to conduct large-scale, single-center studies on PSC. The exclusion of patients with incomplete data may have introduced selection bias, and other clinical events could impact the reliability of the risk score. Unmeasured confounders also limit the model’s applicability. Also, the single-center approach raises concerns about overfitting. Multi-center studies are needed to confirm the MRS’s broader applicability.

Additionally, while our findings affirm the predictive validity of the MRS, they do not assess its calibration. Despite these limitations, our study highlights the critical need for prolonged observation to deepen the understanding of PSC. Future research should focus on validating the prognostic factors using both retrospective and prospective methodologies and exploring their integration into novel predictive models.

## 5. Conclusions

Our findings indicate that the MRS is a reliable predictor of LT and mortality in patients with recently diagnosed PSC who have not yet progressed to the later stages of the disease. These results address a significant limitation of previous studies that primarily focused on patients with advanced-stage PSC at the baseline assessment. With excellent predictive performance and significant associations with adverse outcomes, the MRS provides a valuable tool for risk stratification in this population. These results support the broader applicability of the MRS beyond end-stage PSC and highlight its potential to guide clinical decision-making and early intervention strategies.
